title: Project Plan: Migration to a New ERP System

content.text: Project Plan: Migration to a New ERP System
1.2, approved by the steering committee on [DATE_1]

This project plan describes how [ORG_1] will replace its current ERP system with a new, cloud-based ERP platform. It defines the objectives, scope, organisation, schedule, budget and risks of the project and serves as the binding reference for all project members, the steering committee and the implementation partner [ORG_2].
The plan is a living document. The project manager updates it at the end of each phase and whenever the steering committee approves a change request. All changes are recorded in the change log on the
. Department heads receive a short summary of each new version by email.

[ORG_1] manufactures industrial valves, actuators and control units for the chemical, water and energy industries. The company employs around 900 people at three sites: the headquarters and main plant in [LOCATION_1], a machining and assembly plant in [LOCATION_2] and a logistics and service centre in [LOCATION_3]. Annual revenue in the last financial year was EUR 214 million, of which 58 percent was generated outside Germany.

The current ERP system was introduced in 2004 and has been extended over the years with more than 400 custom developments. Its manufacturer will end mainstream maintenance at the end of 2027. Many processes rely on spreadsheets and manual workarounds, especially in variant configuration, service management and intercompany invoicing. Month-end closing currently takes eleven working days, and production planners spend a considerable part of their time reconciling data between the ERP system and the manufacturing execution system.

In a preliminary study carried out from January to April, the company evaluated three ERP vendors and selected a cloud-based ERP platform with standard functions for discrete manufacturing and variant configuration. [ORG_2] was selected as implementation partner following a tender with four bidders. The management board approved the business case and the overall budget on [DATE_2].

The business case expects annual savings of around EUR 1.4 million from the third year after go-live. The main drivers are lower maintenance costs for custom developments, the elimination of manual reconciliations between systems, a reduction of inventory through better planning and a shorter month-end closing. In addition, the new system is a prerequisite for the planned introduction of electronic invoicing with customers and suppliers and for the integration of the foreign subsidiaries.
The project aims to replace the legacy system with a standardised, future-proof ERP platform that supports the growth strategy of [ORG_1] until at least 2035. The guiding principle is
: the company adapts its processes to the standard of the new system wherever this is economically reasonable, and custom developments are only permitted if they are approved by the design authority.
The project is considered successful if the following criteria are met:
The go-live of all three sites takes place on [DATE_3] without interruption of deliveries to customers for more than two working days.
At least 85 percent of the business processes are mapped in the standard of the new system.
The number of custom developments is reduced from more than 400 to fewer than 40.
Month-end closing is shortened from eleven to six working days within six months after go-live.
The total project budget of EUR 6.8 million is not exceeded by more than 5 percent.
At least 90 percent of key users rate the training as good or very good.

The scope is defined at the level of business processes and sites. Any extension of the scope requires a change request, which is assessed by the project manager and approved by the steering committee.
Change requests can be submitted by any workstream lead using the template in the project document library. They are processed as follows:
The workstream lead describes the requested change, the business reason and the consequences of not implementing it.
The project manager and [ORG_2] assess the impact on schedule, budget, resources and risks within ten working days.
The design authority checks whether the change is compatible with the standard-first principle.
Changes with an impact of up to EUR 25,000 and no effect on the go-live date are approved by the project sponsor.
All other changes are submitted to the steering committee for decision at its next meeting.
Approved changes are recorded in the change log and included in the next version of this project plan.

These remain in the existing HR system and are connected via a cost centre interface.
The sales companies in France, Poland and the United States will follow in a separate rollout project from 2028.
The existing CRM system remains in place; only the interface to the new ERP system is part of the project.
Data older than three years is archived by IT operations in a separate workstream with its own budget.

The project is organised as a joint project between [ORG_1] and [ORG_2]. Each business workstream is led by a workstream lead from [ORG_1] and supported by a consultant from the implementation partner. Key users from the departments are released from their daily work for 30 to 50 percent of their working time during the design and test phases.

It consists of the CFO [PERSON_1] (chair), the Chief Operating Officer [PERSON_3], the Head of IT [PERSON_4] and the managing director of [ORG_2], [PERSON_5]. The works council receives regular information on the project status in accordance with the Works Constitution Act.

The core team of [ORG_1] comprises 14 full-time equivalents, including the project manager, five workstream leads, a data migration lead, two IT architects and five key users released for the full duration of the project. A further 35 key users contribute part-time. [ORG_2] provides a team of up to twelve consultants, with an average of eight consultants on site or remotely during the realisation phase.

Department heads have confirmed the release of their key users in writing. If a key user leaves the company or is absent for an extended period, the department head nominates a substitute within two weeks and ensures the handover of open tasks.

The project follows a phased approach with five phases. Each phase ends with a quality gate at which the steering committee decides whether the project may proceed to the next phase. The criteria for each quality gate are defined in the

The phases build on each other, but realisation sprints for less complex process areas may start while the design of other areas is still being finalised. Overlaps of this kind must be approved by the design authority.
project set-up, onboarding of the implementation partner, detailed planning and provisioning of the system landscape.
fit-to-standard workshops for all process areas, documentation of the target processes and decisions on gaps.
configuration, custom developments, interfaces and data migration in iterative sprints of three weeks each.
integration tests, user acceptance tests, two migration rehearsals and end-user training.
cutover, go-live at all sites and eight weeks of intensive support.

, the project team sets up the project infrastructure, including the document library, the ticket system for project issues and the development, test and quality assurance systems provided by the ERP vendor. [ORG_2] conducts onboarding sessions for the core team on the methodology and the basic navigation of the new system. The detailed plan for the design phase, including the schedule of all workshops, is agreed with the department heads.

, more than 60 fit-to-standard workshops are held. In each workshop, consultants of [ORG_2] demonstrate the standard process in a preconfigured system, and the key users identify gaps between the standard and the requirements of [ORG_1]. Each gap is documented and classified as "adapt the process", "configure", "develop" or "reject". The phase ends with the approval of the target process design by the process owners.

, the system is configured in three-week sprints. At the end of each sprint, the workstreams present the results to the key users in a sprint review. Custom developments approved by the design authority are developed in parallel by the development team of [ORG_2]. The data migration team performs the first test load of master data and validates the results together with the data owners.

, the complete process chains are tested across all workstreams, from the customer quotation to the incoming payment and from the purchase requisition to the supplier payment. Two complete migration rehearsals ensure that the cutover can be executed within the planned time window. End-user training starts once the user acceptance test has been signed off.

, the cutover runbook is executed, the go-live is carried out at all three sites and the project team provides intensive support for eight weeks. During hypercare, the first month-end closing in the new system is supported by consultants of [ORG_2]. At the end of the phase, open tickets, documentation and system responsibility are handed over to IT operations and the business application support team.
Interfaces to MES and PDM tested
End of hypercare and handover to IT operations

The go-live date has been chosen to coincide with the start of a new financial quarter and the planned production shutdown over the holidays, which reduces the operational risk of the cutover. If quality gate 3 is not passed, the next possible go-live window is three months later.

All three sites will go live on the same weekend ("big bang"). A phased go-live by site was evaluated but rejected, because the sites share a common material master, intercompany flows and a central warehouse, and temporary interfaces between the old and new systems would have cost an estimated EUR 450,000 without reducing the overall risk significantly.

The cutover is planned over four days. Production in [LOCATION_1] and [LOCATION_2] stops on the Thursday before go-live, and the last deliveries are shipped from the logistics centre on Friday morning. Open orders, stock levels and open items are migrated over the weekend, and the new system is available to all users on Monday at 6:00 a.m. A detailed cutover runbook with more than 300 tasks will be prepared during the testing phase and rehearsed twice.

The data migration is one of the most critical parts of the project. Only data that is required for operational business after go-live is migrated; historical transactions remain accessible in a read-only archive of the legacy system for ten years in accordance with statutory retention obligations under the German Commercial Code (HGB) and tax law.
The following data objects are migrated:
materials, bills of materials, routings, work centres, customers, suppliers and price conditions
open sales orders, purchase orders, production orders, service orders and quotations valid for more than 30 days
opening balances of the general ledger, open items of customers and suppliers, fixed assets with their acquisition values and accumulated depreciation
stock levels per storage location, batch and serial number at the time of cutover

Each data object has a data owner in the business department who is responsible for cleansing the data in the legacy system and for approving the migration results. The data migration lead coordinates the migration tooling, the mapping rules and the reconciliation reports. A migration test load is only accepted if at least 98 percent of records are loaded without errors and all financial balances reconcile with the legacy system.
The quality of the new system is ensured through a multi-stage test concept. Each test stage has defined entry and exit criteria, and defects are recorded and tracked in the project ticket system.
carried out by [ORG_2] for each configuration item and custom development during the sprints.
two test cycles covering all end-to-end processes and interfaces, carried out by the workstreams with support from the key users.
carried out by the key users and approved by the process owners for their area.
simulation of peak load at month-end closing with 250 concurrent users.
two complete dress rehearsals of the cutover, including the measurement of runtimes for all migration steps.

The exit criterion for go-live is that there are no open defects of priority 1 and no more than ten open defects of priority 2, each with an agreed workaround. The test manager reports the test progress and defect status weekly to the project meeting and monthly to the steering committee.

Risks are recorded in the project risk register, assessed by probability and impact and reviewed in the weekly project meeting. Risks with a high rating are escalated to the steering committee. The most important risks at the start of the project are:

Key users may not be sufficiently released from their daily work, especially during the peak season from March to June. Mitigation: written release agreements, backfilling with temporary staff in sales administration and monthly monitoring of time bookings.

The material master contains around 180,000 records, of which an estimated 30 percent are outdated or duplicated. Mitigation: a data cleansing workstream starts in the preparation phase, and data owners are named for each master data object.
The configuration logic for the actuator product line is complex and only partly documented. Mitigation: a dedicated sprint, early prototype and involvement of the product management team.
The interface to the manufacturing execution system is critical for production. Mitigation: early technical proof of concept and end-to-end tests with real production orders.
Long-standing employees are used to the old system and its custom functions. Mitigation: a change management plan, early involvement of team leaders and a network of change agents at all sites.
A delay beyond the planned date would extend parallel maintenance costs for the legacy system. Mitigation: contingency of three weeks in the plan and a clearly defined fallback go-live window.

Each risk is rated on a scale from 1 to 5 for probability and impact. Risks with a total score of 15 or more are classified as high and require a named risk owner, a mitigation plan with deadlines and monthly reporting to the steering committee. Risks that have materialised are transferred to the issue log and handled with priority.

A fallback plan will be defined for the go-live weekend. It describes the criteria under which the cutover is aborted and the legacy system is reactivated. The decision on a rollback is taken by the steering committee no later than Sunday at 6:00 p.m.

The introduction of a new ERP system changes the daily work of around 600 users. The project therefore includes a dedicated change management workstream led by [PERSON_7] from human resources. Its objective is to ensure that employees understand why the change is necessary, what will change for them and where they can get help.

Training follows a train-the-trainer approach. [ORG_2] trains the key users, who in turn train the end users in their departments. Each end user receives role-based training of between four hours and three days, depending on their role. Training materials, short videos and quick reference guides are made available on the
. Training takes place no earlier than six weeks before go-live, so that the knowledge is still fresh on the first day.

A network of around 40 change agents supports the workstream. Change agents are respected employees from all departments and shifts who pass on information to their colleagues, collect questions and concerns and report the mood in their teams back to the project. They meet every four weeks with the change management lead and receive early access to demonstrations of the new system.

During hypercare, floor walkers will be present at each site during the first two weeks after go-live. A central support desk staffed by key users and consultants of [ORG_2] will handle all requests. Tickets are prioritised according to their impact on deliveries and production.
Regular and transparent communication is essential for the acceptance of the project. The communication activities are planned as follows:

Status reports use a traffic light system for schedule, budget, scope, quality and risks. A red status in any area must be explained, together with the corrective measures and the support required from the steering committee.

The total budget approved by the management board amounts to EUR 6.8 million for the period until the end of hypercare. It includes external services, licences for the first year, internal personnel costs and a contingency of 10 percent.

Budget control is carried out monthly by the project controller. The use of the contingency requires the approval of the project sponsor for amounts up to EUR 100,000 and of the steering committee for higher amounts. Licence costs from the second year onwards are part of the regular IT budget.

The project controller also tracks the realisation of the benefits defined in the business case. A benefits review will take place twelve months after go-live, in which the actual savings are compared with the planned values and further optimisation measures are agreed with the process owners.
This plan is based on the following assumptions. If one of them turns out to be wrong, the project manager assesses the consequences and informs the steering committee.
The ERP vendor provides the cloud system landscape within four weeks of contract signature.
No other major IT projects are carried out at [ORG_1] during the realisation and testing phases.
The upgrade of the manufacturing execution system planned by production IT is completed before the start of the integration tests.
Key users are available to the agreed extent and are not deployed in other projects.
The legacy system remains fully operational and supported until the end of hypercare.
